solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Send up Times campaign?

parts.note: to lob is to send something up high in an arc
BY as in multiplication: three by four is three times four

explanation.surface: A sarcastic suggestion that someone mock the Times newspaper as a kind of campaign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Send up' looks like mockery, but it means to throw upwards; 'Times' is the multiplication sign read aloud as BY.
explanation.definitionFit: To lobby is to campaign by pressing politicians for a cause, a common political verb.

clue.text: Politician, unusually calm deliberator

indicators.note: done unusually, the letters of the fodder are put in an unfamiliar order

explanation.surface: A politician described as an unusually calm deliberator, a rarity in parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: A Liberal Democrat is a member of the British Liberal Democrats party.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of the UK's centrist Liberal Democrat party is a kind of politician.

clue.text: Flyers to rip off? Someone's might be saved

parts.note: BA is British Airways, whose aircraft fly passengers
to con someone is to cheat or rip them off

explanation.surface: Asking whether an airline would rip someone off, though a person might still be rescued.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on the idiom 'save one's bacon', to escape harm narrowly.
explanation.definitionFit: In the idiom 'save your bacon' it is the thing that gets rescued, so this cured pork is what someone's might be.

clue.text: Buy sets for modelling: they come with reservations?

indicators.note: modelling reshapes material, so the given letters are moulded into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone buys sets for modelling, but the purchases come with certain conditions.
explanation.definitionFit: A 'yes, but' is a response agreeing with an objection attached, so these replies carry qualifications or doubts.

clue.text: Spot if the criminal makes call after crime

indicators.note: criminal suggests something crooked or bent, so the letters are twisted into a new order

explanation.surface: Seeing a criminal makes a bystander shout a warning after the crime.
explanation.definitionFit: The cry 'Stop thief!' is the traditional shout raised after a robbery to get help catching the culprit.

clue.text: State of regularly neglected wreaths revolting

indicators.note: revolting here means turning over, so the remaining letters are read backwards
every other letter of wreaths is neglected, leaving only the alternate ones

explanation.surface: Wreaths left uncared for at a memorial become a revolting sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly neglected' drops R, A and H from wreaths, leaving WETS; 'revolting' then turns WETS round.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in a stew is to be in an agitated condition, so the word means a state of anxiety.

clue.text: Jolly entertaining drama, overwhelming in arena?

indicators.note: entertaining in the sense of hosting a guest, so one piece holds the other within it

parts.note: a jolly is a pleasure trip or outing
a play is a drama

explanation.surface: A cheerful drama being described as entertaining, overpowering in a theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jolly' looks like an adjective, but in British English a jolly is a fun excursion.
explanation.definitionFit: Outplaying an opponent means beating them comprehensively in a game, as on a sports field or arena.

clue.text: Like Katherine's mother to have food served all round

indicators.note: the food sits all round the mother, enclosing her

parts.note: a table can mean the food provided, as in 'she keeps a good table'
ma is an informal word for mother

explanation.surface: Katherine's mother has a meal brought out for everyone present.
explanation.walkthrough: Katherine is the shrew in Shakespeare's The Taming of the Shrew, who is eventually tamed.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's heroine Katherine is subdued by Petruchio, so she proves capable of being tamed.

clue.text: Lion following, being after one's territory

indicators.note: after says the lion, following and being come behind the one's

parts.note: one is I, so one's is I'S, written IS
Leo is the lion of the zodiac
F is the abbreviation for following, as in page references
a man is a human being

explanation.surface: A lion follows another creature onto some territory it claims as its own.
explanation.walkthrough: The Isle of Man is a self-governing British Crown dependency in the Irish Sea.
explanation.definitionFit: The island is a Crown dependency, a territory with its own parliament though not part of the UK.

clue.text: New storefronts met with mockery at first throughout

indicators.note: new means made afresh, so the letters are rearranged
at first takes only the opening letter of mockery

explanation.surface: New shop fronts were greeted with derision at first all over town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' takes STOREFRONTS, MET and M (the first letter of mockery, signalled by 'at first') and rearranges all fifteen letters together.
explanation.definitionFit: Stem and stern are a ship's front and back, so the phrase means from end to end, entirely.

clue.text: Champions were upset, sloping off to the rear

parts.note: to champion a cause is to back it, so champions means backs
wept means cried, as people do when upset

explanation.surface: Champions were upset after a fall that sent them off backwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Champions' reads as a noun for winners, but it is the verb meaning supports.
explanation.definitionFit: Backswept describes something angled backwards, like swept-back hair or aircraft wings.

clue.text: Very short saying: time to go for length

indicators.note: one letter is to go, replaced by another

parts.note: a motto is a short pithy saying

explanation.surface: A brief phrase advising it is time to leave, considering the distance.
explanation.walkthrough: Molto is the Italian musical direction meaning very, as in molto allegro.
explanation.definitionFit: The musical term from Italian intensifies a tempo marking, just as the English adverb does.

clue.text: To be exhausted after race not acceptable

indicators.note: after puts the second piece behind the race

parts.note: a run is a race
out means unfashionable or not allowed

explanation.surface: Collapsing with tiredness after a race is not acceptable for an athlete.
explanation.definitionFit: Supplies run out when used up, so the phrasal verb means become depleted or used up.

clue.text: Wellington Arch is in front of small fox

indicators.note: says the arch piece stands before the wellington and small

parts.note: arch as an adjective means knowing or mischievous, i.e. sly
a wellington is a rubber boot
S is the abbreviation for small, as in clothing sizes

explanation.surface: London's Wellington Arch stands in front of a small fox.
explanation.walkthrough: Wellington Arch is a London landmark, but here Wellington is a boot and Arch means cunning.
explanation.definitionFit: A fox is a cunning person, and a slyboots is a crafty, wily individual.

clue.text: Food items for battering in the kitchen?

definitions.text: Food items for battering in the kitchen?

parts.words: Food items for battering in the kitchen?
parts.note: chicken legs that may be coated in batter, but also the sticks a percussionist uses to batter a drum kit

explanation.walkthrough: 'battering' suggests coating food in batter for frying, but it also means beating, and a drum 'kit' hides in 'kitchen'.
explanation.definitionFit: Poultry legs are a common food item, and the same word names the beaters for a drum.

clue.text: Unruly players' union blocks invitation from minister

indicators.note: the union blocks the players by sitting in the middle of them
unruly means disorderly, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: TU is the abbreviation for trade union

explanation.surface: A disorderly players' union obstructs a request from a government minister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minister' suggests politics, but here it is a member of the clergy leading a church service.
explanation.definitionFit: A clergyman leading worship says these words to invite the congregation to pray together.

clue.text: Distant waves and cheers when minister's house opens

indicators.note: the cheers opens up to admit the other pieces

parts.note: ta is British informal for thanks, like cheers
as can mean when, as in 'as he arrived'
a manse is a Scottish minister's house

explanation.surface: Faraway waves and cheers as a minister's house opens to the public.
explanation.walkthrough: 'opens' reads as the house opening its doors, but it is the cheers word that is opened up to hold the rest. A manse is the home of a Scottish Presbyterian minister.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tasman Sea lies between Australia and New Zealand, distant waters from a British viewpoint.

clue.text: Girl welcoming yours truly in at four o'clock?

indicators.note: welcoming means taking in a guest, so one piece holds the other

parts.note: on a clock face with twelve as north, four o'clock points east-south-east
yours truly is the speaker, i.e. me

explanation.surface: A girl invites the speaker in for afternoon tea at four.
explanation.walkthrough: Treat the clock face as a compass: twelve is north, three is east, so four o'clock is ESE.
explanation.definitionFit: Esmee is a female first name, so it fits as a girl's name.

clue.text: Classic venue where doctor's exercising back

indicators.note: back means the letters run in reverse order

parts.note: MO is a medical officer, a doctor, so doctor's is MO'S
PE is physical education, exercising

explanation.surface: A famous place where a doctor is doing his workout once again.
explanation.walkthrough: Epsom Downs hosts the Derby and the Oaks, two of the five British horse-racing classics.
explanation.definitionFit: The Surrey racecourse stages the Derby, one of the flat-racing Classics, making it a venue for those races.

clue.text: Confusion, with religious festival returning as new

parts.note: a mela is a Hindu religious fair or festival

indicators.note: returning sends these letters back the other way

parts.note: as in 'such as', the same as e.g., for example

explanation.surface: Chaos ensues as a religious festival comes back looking as good as new.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as' stands for e.g., as in 'cities such as Paris'; a mela is a Hindu fair held at a holy site.
explanation.definitionFit: A melange is a jumbled mixture, a muddle of different things.

clue.text: Vital during day teachers should get a little food

indicators.note: the vital piece comes during, i.e. in the course of, the day's piece

parts.note: Mon is the abbreviation for Monday
key means crucial or vital
NUT is the National Union of Teachers

explanation.surface: It is vital that teachers get a small snack during the school day.
explanation.walkthrough: The NUT was the main British teachers' trade union.
explanation.definitionFit: A monkey nut is a peanut in its shell, a small snack.

clue.text: Was previously top, top journalist

parts.note: ex means former or previously
top means first, written 1ST and read as IST
an editor, ED, is the senior journalist on a paper

explanation.surface: Someone who was once the best is now a leading journalist.
explanation.walkthrough: The digit 1 in 1ST is read as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: Both verbs describe having been in being, so the past tense of exist can replace was.

clue.text: Plea to sleep in? So easily achieved!

parts.note: O is the vocative interjection used when pleading, as in 'O, let me'
to nap late is to sleep in

explanation.surface: A request to stay in bed longer, granted with ridiculous ease.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as the plea 'O, nap late!', a call to have a lie-in.
explanation.definitionFit: Something handed to you on a plate comes without effort, so the idiom means gained with no struggle.

clue.text: The Dutch avoid the UK?

definitions.note: 'my old Dutch' is Cockney slang for one's wife

parts.note: to miss is to avoid
from a British setter's point of view, the UK is us

explanation.surface: The people of the Netherlands staying away from Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Dutch' looks like the nationality, but 'my old Dutch' (from duchess) is Cockney for a wife.
explanation.definitionFit: Missus is an informal word for a wife, the same sense as the Cockney 'old Dutch'.

clue.text: What launches spacemen do in craft

indicators.note: what launches a word is its first letter

parts.note: to do in is to kill

explanation.surface: Astronauts being murdered aboard a spacecraft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'craft' looks like a spaceship, but it means expertise.
explanation.definitionFit: Craft and skill are synonyms for expertise or ability in doing something.

clue.text: Left after expected time with others

indicators.note: the left piece comes after the expected time

parts.note: ETA is estimated time of arrival

explanation.surface: Someone left after the expected time along with the rest of the group.
explanation.definitionFit: Et al is the Latin abbreviation, used in citations, meaning 'and other people'.

clue.text: Close to harbour, sailor in coat bows

indicators.note: the close of harbour is its last letter

parts.note: OS is ordinary seaman, a sailor

explanation.surface: A sailor near the harbour wears a coat and bows politely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bows' suggests a sailor bending forward or a ship's front, but it is violin bows.
explanation.definitionFit: String players rub resin onto their bows, so to rosin is to coat them with it.

clue.text: Take risks to manage punishment

parts.note: to cut it is to cope or manage, as in 'can he cut it?'
a fine is a monetary punishment

explanation.surface: Taking risks in order to deal with a penalty.
explanation.definitionFit: To cut it fine is to leave a very small margin, especially of time, which is chancy.

clue.text: Coming across short story about party-goers

indicators.note: the trimmed story goes about the party-goers, surrounding them
short means cut, so the tale loses its last letter

parts.note: a tale is a story
ravers go to parties

explanation.surface: A brief tale about clubbers crossing the room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coming across' looks like part of the story's action, but it is the definition: the act of crossing.
explanation.definitionFit: A traversal is the act of crossing over something, a passage from one side to the other.

clue.text: The writer Thomas Hardy languishes, greatly diminished

indicators.note: the two words are greatly reduced, leaving only a short run of letters across them

explanation.surface: Thomas Hardy, the novelist, wastes away and is much reduced.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites Thomas Hardy, but the writer wanted is the Welsh poet Dylan Thomas.
explanation.definitionFit: Dylan Thomas was the Welsh poet who wrote Under Milk Wood, a writer named Thomas.
